screens.title: Data in Transit: Why Encryption Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Data in transit, often called data in motion, refers to any data actively moving from one location to another. This could be data traveling across a public network like the internet, moving between different applications within your cloud environment, or even flowing between your on-premises data centers and Azure. Think of it as a digital package being delivered. Just as a physical package can be intercepted or tampered with during delivery, digital data is vulnerable to various attacks while it's in motion. Without proper encryption, this data is susceptible to eavesdropping, where unauthorized parties can listen in and steal sensitive information. It's also at risk of tampering, where data can be altered or corrupted, and man-in-the-middle attacks, where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters the communication between two parties who believe they are directly communicating. Therefore, securing data in transit is just as critical as securing data at rest, forming a fundamental pillar of a comprehensive security strategy. It ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity throughout the data's journey, safeguarding your organization's most valuable assets. Module 3›Chapter 2›Data in Transit: Why Encryption Matters
Core Concept

Data in Transit: Why Encryption Matters

Protecting information as it moves across networks.

What is Data in Transit?

Data in transit, or data in motion, refers to any data actively moving from one location to another. This includes data traversing public networks, flowing between applications, or moving between on-premises environments and cloud services like Azure.

Key Vulnerabilities

  • Eavesdropping: Unauthorized interception of data.
  • Tampering: Malicious alteration or corruption of data.
  • Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attacks: Intercepting and relaying communications between two parties.
Key Takeaway

Securing data in transit is as critical as securing data at rest to maintain confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.

The Journey of Data

From Source to Destination, Securely.

screens.title: Securing Public Endpoints with TLS/SSL
screens.narratorSegment: When data travels over public networks, especially the internet, Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is the most common and fundamental mechanism for encryption. You might also hear it referred to by its older name, SSL. TLS provides a secure channel over a computer network, primarily used for web traffic, which is why you see 'HTTPS' in your browser. Azure services that expose public endpoints, such as Azure App Service for web applications, Azure Front Door for global traffic management, Azure Application Gateway for web traffic load balancing, and Azure A P I Management for A P I gateways, all inherently support TLS. As an architect, your key responsibility is to ensure TLS is properly configured. This means enforcing strong, modern TLS versions, typically TLS 1.2 or higher, to protect against known vulnerabilities. It also involves robust certificate management practices, often leveraging Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your custom domain SSL certificates. For example, with Azure App Service, you can easily bind these certificates to your custom domains, ensuring all traffic to your web application is encrypted. Prioritizing end-to-end encryption, even for traffic within your virtual network, by ensuring backend services also use HTTPS, is a best practice that adds layers of defense.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Securing Public Endpoints with TLS/SSL
Core Mechanism

Securing Public Endpoints with TLS/SSL

The fundamental protocol for encrypted web communication.

What is TLS/SSL?

Transport Layer Security (TLS), and its predecessor Secure Sockets Layer (SSL), are cryptographic protocols designed to provide communication security over a computer network. They are widely used for web traffic (HTTPS) to ensure data confidentiality and integrity.

Azure Service Support

  • Azure App Service: Easily bind custom domain SSL certificates.
  • Azure Front Door: Centralized TLS/SSL offloading at the edge.
  • Azure Application Gateway: Handles encryption/decryption, reducing backend load.
  • Azure API Management: Secures API endpoints.
Key Takeaway

Always enforce modern TLS versions (1.2+) and manage certificates securely for all public-facing Azure services.

TLS/SSL in Action

Encrypting the connection from client to Azure endpoint.

Client Browser

Azure App Service

TLS ensures secure, authenticated, and encrypted communication between clients and Azure public endpoints.

screens.title: Centralized TLS Offloading with Azure Front Door and Application Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: Managing TLS encryption and decryption can be resource-intensive for your backend web servers. This is where centralized TLS offloading comes into play, a powerful feature offered by Azure Front Door and Azure Application Gateway. These services act as a 'front door' or 'gateway' to your applications, handling the encryption and decryption of TLS traffic at the edge of the network. By offloading this computational burden, your backend web servers can focus on processing application logic, leading to improved performance and scalability. For example, Azure Front Door, a global, scalable entry-point, can terminate TLS connections at the closest edge location to the user, reducing latency and improving response times. Similarly, Azure Application Gateway, a regional web traffic load balancer, can perform TLS termination before forwarding unencrypted (or re-encrypted) traffic to your backend pools. This approach also simplifies certificate management, as you only need to manage certificates on the gateway service, rather than on every individual backend server. However, it's crucial to remember that while offloading is efficient, you should always prioritize end-to-end encryption. This means ensuring that even the traffic from the gateway to your backend services within your virtual network is re-encrypted using HTTPS, maintaining a strong security posture throughout the entire data path.

Azure Service Feature

Centralized TLS Offloading

Optimizing performance and simplifying certificate management.

What is TLS Offloading?

TLS offloading is the process where a dedicated device or service, like Azure Front Door or Application Gateway, handles the encryption and decryption of TLS traffic, reducing the computational load on backend web servers.

Benefits of Centralization

  • Performance Boost: Backend servers focus on application logic.
  • Simplified Management: Certificates managed in one place.
  • Enhanced Security: Consistent TLS policy enforcement.
Key Takeaway

Always ensure end-to-end encryption, even when using TLS offloading, by re-encrypting traffic to backend services.

screens.title: Secure Hybrid Connectivity with Azure VPN Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: For organizations needing to securely connect their on-premises data centers with Azure, hybrid connectivity solutions are essential. One of the primary solutions is the Azure VPN Gateway. A VPN Gateway creates an encrypted tunnel over the public internet, effectively extending your on-premises network into an Azure Virtual Network. This means data flowing between your local environment and Azure is protected from interception and tampering, even though it traverses the public internet. There are two main types of VPNs to consider: Site-to-Site VPNs, which connect entire networks, allowing resources in both locations to communicate securely as if they were on the same network. Then there are Point-to-Site VPNs, which enable individual client machines, like a remote employee's laptop, to connect securely to Azure. VPNs leverage IPsec for robust encryption and authentication, ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of your data. While VPNs are a cost-effective and relatively straightforward solution to set up, their performance and reliability can be influenced by public internet conditions. This makes them suitable for many scenarios, but perhaps not for the most mission-critical applications requiring guaranteed performance. Understanding these distinctions helps you choose the right tool for your hybrid architecture.

Hybrid Solution

Secure Hybrid Connectivity with Azure VPN Gateway

Encrypted tunnels over the public internet for network extension.

What is Azure VPN Gateway?

An Azure VPN Gateway creates an encrypted tunnel over the public internet, establishing a secure connection between your on-premises network and an Azure Virtual Network. It uses IPsec for encryption and authentication.

Types of VPNs

  • Site-to-Site VPNs: Connect entire on-premises networks to Azure Virtual Networks.
  • Point-to-Site VPNs: Allow individual client machines to connect securely to Azure.
Key Takeaway

VPNs are cost-effective for hybrid connectivity, but their performance can be subject to public internet conditions.

screens.title: Azure ExpressRoute: Dedicated Private Connections
screens.narratorSegment: While Azure VPN Gateways offer a flexible and cost-effective solution for hybrid connectivity, some mission-critical applications demand higher performance, lower latency, and greater reliability. For these scenarios, Azure ExpressRoute is the preferred solution. ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection between your on-premises infrastructure and Azure, completely bypassing the public internet. This dedicated connection is established through a connectivity provider, offering predictable performance and guaranteed bandwidth, which is crucial for workloads like large data transfers, real-time applications, or database replication. Unlike VPNs, ExpressRoute is not subject to internet congestion or variability, making it ideal for enterprise-grade solutions. However, it's a common misconception that because ExpressRoute is a private connection, data is automatically encrypted end-to-end at the application layer. While the physical connection is private, for highly sensitive data, it's still best practice to implement additional encryption. This could involve MACsec at the physical layer, or more commonly, IPsec tunnels over ExpressRoute to ensure end-to-end encryption of the data payload. This layered approach provides the highest level of security, even over a dedicated private link, ensuring your most sensitive data remains protected.

Module 3›Chapter 2›Azure ExpressRoute: Dedicated Private Connections
Premium Hybrid Solution

Azure ExpressRoute: Dedicated Private Connections

High-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity bypassing the public internet.

What is Azure ExpressRoute?

ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection between your on-premises infrastructure and Azure over a connectivity provider. It bypasses the public internet, offering superior reliability, lower latency, and higher bandwidth.

Key Advantages

  • Higher Bandwidth: Up to 100 Gbps.
  • Lower Latency: Predictable and consistent network performance.
  • Enhanced Reliability: Dedicated private connection, not subject to internet conditions.
  • Bypasses Public Internet: Reduces exposure to internet-based threats.
Key Takeaway

Even with ExpressRoute, consider additional encryption (e.g., IPsec tunnels) for highly sensitive data.

ExpressRoute Architecture

Private, dedicated path to Azure.

ExpressRoute offers a dedicated, high-performance path, ideal for demanding hybrid cloud workloads.

screens.title: Controlling Traffic Flow with Network Security Groups (NSGs)
screens.narratorSegment: Within Azure Virtual Networks, Network Security Groups, or NSGs, are fundamental for controlling traffic flow and enforcing security policies. Think of an NSG as a firewall that operates at a very granular level, either at the network interface card, or NIC, level of an individual virtual machine, or at the subnet level, affecting all resources within that subnet. NSGs filter traffic based on a set of rules that you define, specifying source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols. For example, you can create a rule to allow inbound SSH traffic only from a specific management IP range, or deny all outbound traffic to the internet except for specific ports. While NSGs are crucial for creating secure network segmentation, which limits the scope of potential breaches by isolating different parts of your network, it's important to understand a key distinction: NSGs do not inherently encrypt data. Their role is to filter and control access, not to encrypt the data payload itself. They are a foundational security layer that works in conjunction with encryption mechanisms to build a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy. By segmenting your network effectively with NSGs, you reduce the attack surface and contain threats, even if an initial breach occurs.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Controlling Traffic Flow with Network Security Groups (NSGs)
Network Control

Controlling Traffic Flow with Network Security Groups (NSGs)

Filtering network traffic at the subnet and NIC level.

What are NSGs?

Network Security Groups (NSGs) are Azure resources that contain security rules allowing or denying inbound and outbound network traffic. They filter traffic based on source/destination IP, port, and protocol at the network interface (NIC) or subnet level.

Role in Security

  • Network Segmentation: Isolate subnets and VMs to limit breach scope.
  • Access Control: Define precise rules for allowed traffic.
  • Defense-in-Depth: A foundational layer, but does not encrypt data.
Key Takeaway

NSGs are essential for traffic filtering and segmentation, but they do not provide data encryption.

NSG Rule Evaluation

Traffic flow based on priority and direction.

screens.title: Azure Firewall: Centralized Network Security
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the granular control offered by NSGs, Azure Firewall provides a more advanced, managed, cloud-based network security service. Think of Azure Firewall as a centralized security appliance for all your Azure Virtual Network resources. It offers a higher level of threat protection and control compared to NSGs, making it ideal for perimeter security and securing hub-and-spoke architectures. Key features include FQDN filtering, which allows you to filter outbound HTTP/S traffic based on fully qualified domain names, not just IP addresses. It also provides network rule collections for traditional firewall rules and application rule collections for more advanced application-layer filtering. screens.title: Deep Packet Inspection with Azure Firewall TLS Inspection
screens.narratorSegment: While Azure Firewall provides robust filtering, many threats are hidden within encrypted traffic. This is where Azure Firewall's TLS inspection feature, available with Azure Firewall Premium, becomes incredibly powerful. TLS inspection allows the firewall to decrypt outbound TLS traffic, inspect it for hidden threats, and then re-encrypt it before forwarding it to its destination. Imagine a security guard who can not only check the exterior of a package but also open it, inspect its contents, and then reseal it before it continues its journey. This deep packet inspection capability is crucial for identifying malware, data exfiltration attempts, or other malicious activities that would otherwise be invisible within encrypted streams. For example, if an employee's machine is compromised and attempts to communicate with a command-and-control server over HTTPS, TLS inspection can detect this malicious traffic. However, implementing TLS inspection requires careful design and management of certificates, as the firewall acts as an intermediary, presenting its own certificate to the client. This feature significantly enhances your security posture, providing an additional layer of defense against sophisticated threats, but it demands meticulous planning to ensure seamless operation and trust within your environment.

screens.title: Common Mistake: Private Network ≠ Encrypted Data
screens.narratorSegment: A very common and dangerous misconception in cloud security design is assuming that simply having a private network connection, such as Azure ExpressRoute, means your data is automatically encrypted end-to-end at the application layer. While ExpressRoute does provide a private, dedicated path that bypasses the public internet, the data itself is not encrypted by default at the application layer. This means that if an attacker were to gain access to the connectivity provider's network, or if there was a compromise within your own network segment connected to ExpressRoute, your sensitive data could still be exposed in clear text. Therefore, for highly sensitive data, architects must still enforce application-level encryption. This means using protocols like HTTPS for web traffic, SMB encryption for file shares, or even implementing IPsec tunnels over ExpressRoute for an additional layer of payload encryption. The private nature of ExpressRoute provides network isolation and performance benefits, but it doesn't replace the need for cryptographic protection of the data itself. Always remember that network security and data encryption are distinct but complementary layers of defense. Relying solely on network isolation for data confidentiality is a critical oversight that can lead to significant security breaches.

Common Mistake: Private Network ≠ Encrypted Data

Understanding that private connections don't automatically encrypt application data.

The Misconception

Many assume that a private network connection, such as Azure ExpressRoute, inherently encrypts data at the application layer. This is incorrect; ExpressRoute provides network isolation but does not encrypt the data payload by default.

Why Application-Layer Encryption is Needed

  • End-to-End Protection: Ensures data is encrypted from source to destination.
  • Defense-in-Depth: Protects against compromises within the private network or provider's network.
  • Compliance: Meets regulatory requirements for sensitive data.
Key Takeaway

Always enforce application-level encryption (e.g., HTTPS, SMB encryption, IPsec) for sensitive data, even over private connections.

Private vs. Encrypted

Network isolation is not data encryption.

screens.title: Common Mistake: Using Outdated TLS Versions and Weak Ciphers
screens.narratorSegment: Another critical mistake in designing data in transit encryption is the continued use of outdated TLS versions or weak cipher suites. Protocols like TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known security vulnerabilities, such as POODLE and BEAST attacks, and are no longer considered secure for protecting sensitive data. Using them leaves your applications and data exposed to significant risks. As an architect, it is imperative to always configure your services to use the latest TLS versions, specifically TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 if available and supported, and to enforce strong cipher suites. Modern TLS versions incorporate stronger cryptographic algorithms and better protection against various attacks. Regularly auditing your TLS configurations is also a best practice. Tools like SSL Labs can help you assess the security of public endpoints, identifying outdated protocols or weak ciphers that need remediation. Furthermore, ensure that all endpoints, whether internal or external, are properly authenticated using certificates or other strong authentication mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access and establish trust. By proactively upgrading and auditing your TLS configurations, you significantly enhance the security posture of your data in transit, aligning with industry best practices and regulatory requirements. This is a continuous effort, not a one-time setup.

Module 3›Chapter 2›Common Mistake: Using Outdated TLS Versions and Weak Ciphers
Security Best Practice

Common Mistake: Using Outdated TLS Versions and Weak Ciphers

Ensuring modern cryptographic protocols for robust security.

Risks of Outdated TLS

  • Known Vulnerabilities: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are susceptible to attacks like POODLE and BEAST.
  • Compliance Issues: Fails to meet industry standards and regulatory requirements.
  • Data Exposure: Increases risk of data interception and decryption.

Best Practices

  • Enforce TLS 1.2+: Configure services to use modern TLS versions.
  • Strong Cipher Suites: Select robust cryptographic algorithms.
  • Regular Audits: Use tools like SSL Labs to check configurations.
  • Endpoint Authentication: Ensure all endpoints are authenticated with certificates.
Key Takeaway

Proactively upgrade and audit TLS configurations to use modern versions and strong ciphers for robust data in transit encryption.

Code Example: Enforce TLS 1.2

Updating Azure App Service minimum TLS version.

# Example: Enforce minimum TLS version for an Azure App Service
# This command updates an existing App Service to require TLS 1.2

APP_SERVICE_NAME="mywebapp-prod-001"
RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME="WebAppRG"

echo "Checking current minimum TLS version for $APP_SERVICE_NAME..."
az webapp config show --name $APP_SERVICE_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME --query minTlsVersion --output tsv

echo "Setting minimum TLS version to 1.2 for $APP_SERVICE_NAME..."
az webapp config set --name $APP_SERVICE_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME --min-tls-version 1.2

echo "Verifying updated minimum TLS version..."
az webapp config show --name $APP_SERVICE_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME --query minTlsVersion --output tsv

This Azure CLI command ensures your App Service enforces a secure TLS protocol version.

Data in transit, often called data in motion, refers to any data actively moving from one location to another. This could be data traveling across a public network like the internet, moving between different applications within your cloud environment, or even flowing between your on-premises data centers and Azure. Think of it as a digital package being delivered. Just as a physical package can be intercepted or tampered with during delivery, digital data is vulnerable to various attacks while it's in motion. Without proper encryption, this data is susceptible to eavesdropping, where unauthorized parties can listen in and steal sensitive information. It's also at risk of tampering, where data can be altered or corrupted, and man-in-the-middle attacks, where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters the communication between two parties who believe they are directly communicating. Therefore, securing data in transit is just as critical as securing data at rest, forming a fundamental pillar of a comprehensive security strategy. It ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity throughout the data's journey, safeguarding your organization's most valuable assets. When data travels over public networks, especially the internet, Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is the most common and fundamental mechanism for encryption. You might also hear it referred to by its older name, SSL. TLS provides a secure channel over a computer network, primarily used for web traffic, which is why you see 'HTTPS' in your browser. Azure services that expose public endpoints, such as Azure App Service for web applications, Azure Front Door for global traffic management, Azure Application Gateway for web traffic load balancing, and Azure A P I Management for A P I gateways, all inherently support TLS. As an architect, your key responsibility is to ensure TLS is properly configured. This means enforcing strong, modern TLS versions, typically TLS 1.2 or higher, to protect against known vulnerabilities. It also involves robust certificate management practices, often leveraging Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your custom domain SSL certificates. For example, with Azure App Service, you can easily bind these certificates to your custom domains, ensuring all traffic to your web application is encrypted. Prioritizing end-to-end encryption, even for traffic within your virtual network, by ensuring backend services also use HTTPS, is a best practice that adds layers of defense.

Managing TLS encryption and decryption can be resource-intensive for your backend web servers. This is where centralized TLS offloading comes into play, a powerful feature offered by Azure Front Door and Azure Application Gateway. These services act as a 'front door' or 'gateway' to your applications, handling the encryption and decryption of TLS traffic at the edge of the network. By offloading this computational burden, your backend web servers can focus on processing application logic, leading to improved performance and scalability. For example, Azure Front Door, a global, scalable entry-point, can terminate TLS connections at the closest edge location to the user, reducing latency and improving response times. Similarly, Azure Application Gateway, a regional web traffic load balancer, can perform TLS termination before forwarding unencrypted (or re-encrypted) traffic to your backend pools. This approach also simplifies certificate management, as you only need to manage certificates on the gateway service, rather than on every individual backend server. However, it's crucial to remember that while offloading is efficient, you should always prioritize end-to-end encryption. This means ensuring that even the traffic from the gateway to your backend services within your virtual network is re-encrypted using HTTPS, maintaining a strong security posture throughout the entire data path.

For organizations needing to securely connect their on-premises data centers with Azure, hybrid connectivity solutions are essential. One of the primary solutions is the Azure VPN Gateway. A VPN Gateway creates an encrypted tunnel over the public internet, effectively extending your on-premises network into an Azure Virtual Network. This means data flowing between your local environment and Azure is protected from interception and tampering, even though it traverses the public internet. There are two main types of VPNs to consider: Site-to-Site VPNs, which connect entire networks, allowing resources in both locations to communicate securely as if they were on the same network. Then there are Point-to-Site VPNs, which enable individual client machines, like a remote employee's laptop, to connect securely to Azure. VPNs leverage IPsec for robust encryption and authentication, ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of your data. While VPNs are a cost-effective and relatively straightforward solution to set up, their performance and reliability can be influenced by public internet conditions. This makes them suitable for many scenarios, but perhaps not for the most mission-critical applications requiring guaranteed performance. Understanding these distinctions helps you choose the right tool for your hybrid architecture.

While Azure VPN Gateways offer a flexible and cost-effective solution for hybrid connectivity, some mission-critical applications demand higher performance, lower latency, and greater reliability. For these scenarios, Azure ExpressRoute is the preferred solution. ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection between your on-premises infrastructure and Azure, completely bypassing the public internet. This dedicated connection is established through a connectivity provider, offering predictable performance and guaranteed bandwidth, which is crucial for workloads like large data transfers, real-time applications, or database replication. Unlike VPNs, ExpressRoute is not subject to internet congestion or variability, making it ideal for enterprise-grade solutions. This could involve MACsec at the physical layer, or more commonly, IPsec tunnels over ExpressRoute to ensure end-to-end encryption of the data payload. This layered approach provides the highest level of security, even over a dedicated private link, ensuring your most sensitive data remains protected.

Their role is to filter and control access, not to encrypt the data payload itself. They are a foundational security layer that works in conjunction with encryption mechanisms to build a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy. By segmenting your network effectively with NSGs, you reduce the attack surface and contain threats, even if an initial breach occurs.

This feature significantly enhances your security posture, providing an additional layer of defense against sophisticated threats, but it demands meticulous planning to ensure seamless operation and trust within your environment.

Protocols like TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known security vulnerabilities, such as POODLE and BEAST attacks, and are no longer considered secure for protecting sensitive data. Using them leaves your applications and data exposed to significant risks. As an architect, it is imperative to always configure your services to use the latest TLS versions, specifically TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 if available and supported, and to enforce strong cipher suites. Modern TLS versions incorporate stronger cryptographic algorithms and better protection against various attacks. Regularly auditing your TLS configurations is also a best practice. Tools like SSL Labs can help you assess the security of public endpoints, identifying outdated protocols or weak ciphers that need remediation. Furthermore, ensure that all endpoints, whether internal or external, are properly authenticated using certificates or other strong authentication mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access and establish trust. By proactively upgrading and auditing your TLS configurations, you significantly enhance the security posture of your data in transit, aligning with industry best practices and regulatory requirements. This is a continuous effort, not a one-time setup.

As we conclude this chapter, let's recap the essential concepts for designing robust encryption for data in transit. First, remember that data in transit encryption is the fundamental process of protecting data as it moves across any network, safeguarding it from interception and tampering. This is a non-negotiable aspect of modern security. Second, Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is the cornerstone protocol for securing communication over networks, especially for public web traffic using HTTPS. Ensuring you use modern TLS versions and proper certificate management is paramount. Finally, for hybrid connectivity, you have powerful tools like Azure VPN Gateway, which creates encrypted tunnels over the public internet, and Azure ExpressRoute, which provides a private, dedicated connection. Each has its strengths and use cases, and understanding their differences is key to making informed architectural decisions. These concepts form the bedrock of securing your data in motion.

Continuing our review of key concepts, it's vital to remember the role of network security controls within Azure. Network Security Groups, or NSGs, are essential for filtering traffic at a granular level, enabling secure network segmentation. While NSGs don't encrypt data, they are a critical layer for controlling access. Azure Firewall, on the other hand, provides advanced, centralized network security with features like FQDN filtering and threat intelligence, acting as a robust perimeter defense. For even deeper inspection, Azure Firewall Premium offers TLS inspection, allowing you to decrypt, inspect, and re-encrypt outbound traffic for hidden threats. Finally, always be aware of common vulnerabilities. Never assume private networks automatically encrypt data, and always enforce modern TLS versions and strong cipher suites to protect against known exploits. By integrating these concepts, you can design and implement a comprehensive and resilient data in transit encryption strategy for your Azure solutions.
